job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Zoe Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Oh, my days are a bit chaotic in a good way. I live with my dad Henrik, who teaches maths at a secondary school in Kellby, and I'm up early to apply for analyst jobs. Then I spend the afternoon on my side project, which is setting up little AI-powered spreadsheets for three cafes and a bike repair shop, for tiny fees. I finished economics at Kellby University last summer with a pass and no internship. I use AI tools every single day, for research, code snippets, even planning meals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit disappointed, but fine. I'd say the useful parts are already here, like summaries and drafts, and the rest was marketing. I'd tell friends to use the boring bits and ignore the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, nothing much changes for me. I'd still be applying, still running the cafe sheets. It's a bit like waiting for a bus, I know there's one coming, it's just late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying to 12 or so analyst roles a week and I'd turn my cafe project into a proper tiny business, with a name and an invoice template. I'd ask Dad to introduce me to the school's finance officer for a reference. And I'd learn SQL properly, because every job ad mentions it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I've got savings, no debt, and Dad's happy to have me around. The only thing is impatience, I want to be doing something that counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Would you be disappointed if it fizzled out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plenty of jobs are posted, but they ask for experience everyone says they can't give. And a pass degree, no internship, isn't what recruiters sort for. So I'm doing the experience bit myself, with the cafes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think you haven't had an offer yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the missing piece is proof. A recruiter doesn't care that I know economics, they want to see I've kept someone's books straight. The cafe sheets are proof, even if they're small.

say: The useful parts, like summaries and drafts, are here already; the rest was **marketing**.
Use the boring bits and ignore the hype.
think: Nothing much changes for me, and I'm like someone **late bus**.
My real issue is impatience, not fear.
do: Apply to **12 analyst roles** a week and learn SQL properly.
Turn the cafe project into a proper tiny business with an **invoice template**.
Ask Dad to introduce me to his school's **finance officer** for a reference.
feel: **Calm**, helped by savings, no debt and Dad's backing.
Impatient to do something that counts.
S0.quote: A recruiter doesn't care that I know economics, they want to see I've kept someone's books straight.
fieldNote: She treats AI as a **daily tool**, not a threat, and her calm is well founded.
She names the real gap herself: **proof of work**, not interest.
Side project is practical evidence of adaptability.

steps.text: Apply to 12 analyst roles every week
Learn SQL properly through a free course
Turn the cafe spreadsheets into a small paid service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the fastest change in my lifetime, and we need to be ready for it. Retraining that's actually paid, and rules so firms don't just fire the whole junior layer. I'd make noise about both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a bit of both. The tools help me, but the same tools mean one analyst now does the work of three. Entry jobs are the ones that shrink, and I'm trying to enter. Still, I'd rather be someone who knows how to run the tools than someone they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the cafe automation as a proper service, maybe 20 small clients by next year. I'd apply to firms that are building AI workflows, because they need people who already use it. And I'd take a short course in data privacy, since small shops get nervous about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous in equal parts. It's like standing on a skateboard that's just started to roll. Fun, but you'd better move your feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your project is basically this card. Does it help or hurt you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Junior staff, people who do routine checks, and anyone who does what I'd call the first draft of everything. The people with savings or family can adapt. The ones without those things can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses most in the world on that card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helps me, but only if I move fast. If I wait, the tools get commoditised and everyone's using them. The gap I want to fill is knowing which tool for which small business, and explaining it in plain words.

say: It's the fastest change in my lifetime, and we must be ready with **paid retraining**.
Rules should stop firms firing the whole **junior layer**.
think: The same tools that help me mean one analyst does the work of **three**.
I'd still rather run the tools than be replaced by them.
do: Sell the cafe automation as a **proper service**, aiming for 20 small clients.
Apply to firms building **AI workflows**, who need people who already use it.
Take a short course in **data privacy**, since small shops worry about it.
feel: **Excited and nervous** in equal parts, like a skateboard that just started rolling.
S1.quote: The tools help me, but the same tools mean one analyst now does the work of three.
fieldNote: She sees both sides honestly: the tools are her **edge** and also the threat to entry jobs.
Her niche is plain-language help for **small businesses**.
Mood stays uneasy because her own skills are an advantage, but entry jobs are shrinking.

steps.text: Sell cafe automation as a service to 20 small clients
Apply to firms building AI workflows
Take a short course in data privacy for small shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need income support right away, something like a basic income, plus rules on how fast firms can replace staff. I'd say it online, and I'd say it to my local representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared, and I'd be lying if I said otherwise. If AI does almost any thinking work better and cheaper, then my tools are the same tools that replace me. My cafe clients could just ask the AI themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hands-on with something that lasts, maybe part-time work at the bike repair shop, since I know the owner and he's offered. I'd put every spare euro in savings. I'd also join the campaign for a basic income, and keep using the tools because I'm not about to unlearn them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit dizzy. It feels like the end of a map where the edge is just drawn in. But I'm young, I'm quick and I've got Dad. So not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on day one after the announcement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Day one I'd call Dad, then the bike shop owner, and then I'd read everything I could about what the governments are saying. I'd want to know who's actually making decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does using AI daily make 2028 less scary or more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more scary, honestly, because I know how good the tools are. People who don't use them think of it as a gimmick. I know it isn't. But knowing how it works also helps me see where it needs people, like checking, trust and talking to customers.

say: We need **income support** right away, like a basic income, plus limits on how fast firms replace staff.
think: The tools I use daily are the same tools that **replace me**.
My cafe clients could ask the AI themselves.
do: Take part-time **hands-on work** at the bike repair shop, where the owner already offered.
Join a **basic income** campaign and keep using the tools.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit dizzy, like the edge of a map, but not panicked because Dad's there.
S2.quote: If AI does almost any thinking work better and cheaper, then my tools are the same tools that replace me.
fieldNote: Knowing the tools well makes her **more** scared, not less, which is a sharp insight.
She hedges with **hands-on work**, using 2031 as the robots' timeline.
Politics comes quickly: she links personal risk to public policy.

steps.text: Take part-time repair work at the bike shop
Put every spare euro into savings
Keep using the AI tools daily

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window, so let's use it. Basic income pilots, paid retraining, a tax on firms that replace staff. I'd write that on my blog and to my representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, uneasy but optimistic. In five years I could build something that isn't just a job someone else can switch off, like a small advisory business, or a role with a firm that needs people who check AI work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any first role I'm offered in the next year, and keep the side business running alongside it. I'd save a third of my pay. I'd also pick up a certification in risk or audit, because there'll be a need for humans who sign things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and cautious. It feels like standing at the top of a slide. I want to go down it, I'm just not sure what's at the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay near finance, but toward the checking side. Somebody has to sign off on what the AI produced, and the law will probably want a human name on it. I'd like to be one of those names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in finance, or move away from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm in survival mode. With five I'm in build mode. That's the big difference, and I'd use it to work on my own thing as well as a job.

say: Five years is a real window, so use it for **basic income pilots** and paid retraining.
Firms that replace staff should be taxed.
think: I'm **uneasy but optimistic**, because I could build something that isn't just a job someone can switch off.
A role checking AI work could be mine.
do: Accept any first role in the next year and run the **side business** alongside.
Get a certification in **risk or audit**, where a human must sign off.
feel: **Excited and cautious**, like standing at the top of a slide.
S3.quote: With two years I'm in survival mode. With five I'm in build mode.
fieldNote: She names the difference the extra time makes: **survival versus build**.
Aims at the human **sign-off** role in audit and risk.
Cushion and adaptability keep her only uneasy.

steps.text: Accept the first finance role offered and keep the side business
Save a third of every pay cheque
Study for a risk and audit certificate
Pitch the side business to more shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a gift, a decade to design the system properly. Let's work out what people do with their time and how they're paid when work isn't the main way. I'd actually want to be part of that conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I feel good about it. I'd have a decade to build a real business, and by the time AGI arrives I'd be 33, adaptable, and experienced at working alongside AI. The risk is more that society stalls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job, run the side business, and study for something like a data governance certificate. I'd put money in a global index fund each month, small but steady. I'd stay near Dad and Kellby, and maybe help him with his school's finance system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a sort of buzz. Like having a very long runway before the plane takes off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does this still feel like your problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in the sense that I'd want to shape it. Even with ten years, if everyone relaxes, we hit 2036 with no plan. So I'd stay involved in policy, even just local.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much from now, actually. The plan's the same, build skills, stay flexible, save. Ten years just lets me do it without being frantic.

say: A decade is a gift for designing the system properly, including **how people are paid** when work isn't central.
I'd want to join that conversation.
think: I feel good, because at 33 I'd be adaptable and experienced working **alongside AI**.
The bigger risk is society stalling.
do: Take a first job, run the side business and study for a **data governance** certificate.
Invest a small amount monthly in a global **index fund**.
Stay local and help Dad with his school's **finance system**.
feel: **Calm**, with a buzz, like a very long runway before take-off.
S4.quote: Even with ten years, if everyone relaxes, we hit 2036 with no plan. So I'd stay involved in policy, even just local.
fieldNote: Calm and **civic**: her worry moves from her own job to society's readiness.
Plan barely changes between scenarios, showing consistent adaptable habits.
The index fund shows time makes **investing** realistic.

steps.text: Take a first job and keep the side business going
Study for a data governance certificate
Put a small amount monthly into an index fund
Join local policy discussions about work and pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. It's the one where my tools and my degree both turn into the thing that replaces me, and nobody has a plan. What would help is a basic income that's already legislated, rules that slow down mass replacement, and some way of proving humans checked the work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not scared of the technology, I'm scared of how slowly everyone else moves. I'm happy to learn, I'm happy to build. I just need the people in charge to catch up.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the technology, I'm scared of how slowly everyone else moves.
portrait: Zoe is a **23-year-old** economics graduate living with her dad, a school maths teacher, and running AI spreadsheets for local cafes.
She is **progressive**: she wants basic income, rules on firms and public support.
She is **adaptive**, uses AI daily and builds her own proof of work.
Knowing the tools well makes the 2028 world scarier, but her savings keep her **anxious** rather than alarmed.
With more time she shifts from survival to building, aiming at checking and sign-off roles.
biggestWorry: Her biggest worry is **AGI by 2028**, where her own tools and degree become what replaces her.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income **already in law**, rules slowing mass replacement, and a way to prove humans checked the work.
